title: What Is an Operating System
summary: The OS's two jobs — resource manager and abstraction layer — and the vocabulary interviewers expect you to untangle: multiprogramming, multitasking, timesharing.

slides.markdown:
An **operating system** is the software that sits between raw hardware and every program you run, doing two jobs at once: sharing finite hardware among competing programs, and hiding hardware's ugly details behind clean abstractions.

Think of it like an air-traffic controller and a translator rolled into one: it decides which plane (process) uses the runway (CPU) next, and it hands pilots a simple radio protocol instead of making them read radar directly. This topic gives you the vocabulary — resource manager, abstraction layer, multiprogramming vs multitasking — that every later OS topic assumes you already have.

slides.sectionTitle: Why every computer needs an OS
slides.markdown:
Without an OS, every application would need its own code to talk directly to the disk controller, the network card, and the CPU's scheduling hardware — and two programs running at once would have no referee stopping them from overwriting each other's memory.

The OS exists to solve exactly that: it owns the hardware and lends it out in controlled, time-sliced, memory-isolated pieces. A program never touches a disk sector directly; it calls `open()`/`read()` and the OS translates that into the actual hardware protocol.

This is why even a single-purpose embedded device (a smart thermostat) usually runs a tiny OS or RTOS rather than bare-metal code once it needs to do more than one thing at a time.

slides.sectionTitle: The two jobs of an OS: resource manager + abstraction layer
slides.markdown:
Every OS textbook definition collapses into two responsibilities. As **resource manager**, it decides who gets the CPU, how much memory each process holds, and in what order disk and network requests are served — arbitrating between processes that would otherwise fight over the same finite hardware.

As **abstraction layer**, it replaces messy hardware realities with clean, uniform interfaces: a file instead of raw disk sectors, a socket instead of network card registers, a virtual address space instead of physical RAM addresses.

Interview signal: when asked "what does an OS do," naming both jobs — not just "it manages the computer" — is what separates a memorized answer from an understood one.

slides.sectionTitle: Multiprogramming, multitasking, timesharing — untangling the terms
slides.markdown:
These three terms get used interchangeably in casual speech but mean different things historically. **Multiprogramming** means keeping several jobs in memory so the CPU always has something to run — originally just to avoid idling the CPU while one job waits on I/O, with no expectation of fast switching.

**Multitasking** adds the idea of switching between jobs fast enough that it looks concurrent, even on one CPU core. **Timesharing** is multitasking applied to interactive users — slicing CPU time so finely that multiple people at terminals each feel like they have the machine to themselves.

In modern usage: multiprogramming is the *why* (keep the CPU busy), multitasking is the *how* (fast switching), and timesharing is multitasking's original interactive use case.

slides.sectionTitle: Types of OS: batch, timesharing, real-time, distributed, embedded
slides.markdown:
Different workloads pushed OS design in different directions, and each type optimizes for a different metric.

| Type | Optimizes for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Batch | Throughput, no user waiting | Mainframe payroll runs |
| Timesharing | Fair, responsive access for many users | Classic Unix on a shared server |
| Real-time | Meeting deadlines, not average speed | Pacemaker, anti-lock brakes |
| Distributed | Coordinating many machines as one system | Google's cluster schedulers |
| Embedded | Small footprint, often single-purpose | Router firmware, a smart thermostat |

**How to decide which fits a scenario:** ask what failure looks like — a batch system failing late is wasted compute, a real-time system failing late can be catastrophic, and that difference drives everything else in its design.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: where the OS sits — hardware, kernel, system programs, applications
slides.markdown:
![OS layered stack from hardware to applications](assets/os-layered-stack.svg)

The **kernel** is the innermost layer with privileged hardware access; **system programs** are trusted software shipped with the OS but running like ordinary programs; **applications** sit on top and never touch hardware except through the kernel.

A common confusion this diagram fixes: "the OS" is the kernel plus everything in the system-programs layer — not just the kernel alone (more in the pitfall slide below).

slides.sectionTitle: Hard real-time vs soft real-time, briefly
slides.markdown:
A **hard real-time** system treats a missed deadline as total system failure — an airbag controller that fires 50ms late has failed, full stop, regardless of how correct the computation was. A **soft real-time** system tolerates occasional missed deadlines as degraded quality, not failure — a video call that drops one frame under load is still "working."

This distinction matters because it changes what you're allowed to optimize for: hard real-time systems sacrifice average-case performance and even throughput to guarantee worst-case bounds, while soft real-time systems (and general-purpose OSes) optimize for good average behavior and accept rare misses.

General-purpose OSes like Linux and Windows are neither — their default schedulers give no deadline guarantees at all, which is exactly why dedicated RTOSes exist (covered in depth in Real-Time Scheduling).

**Wrong belief:** "The kernel and the operating system are the same thing."

**Why it's wrong:** the kernel is the privileged core — scheduler, memory manager, drivers — but "operating system" also includes system programs that ship alongside it: the shell, standard libraries, compilers, package managers, init system. This is precisely the Linux-vs-GNU/Linux debate: Linux is a kernel; the OS most people run is that kernel plus a large userland built mostly by the GNU project.

**Correct model:** kernel ⊂ operating system. When an interviewer asks you to compare "operating systems," they usually mean the whole stack — file layout, tooling, userland conventions — not just the kernel's internals.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: hypervisors, containers, and the OS abstraction stretched further
slides.markdown:
A staff-level answer doesn't stop at "kernel manages hardware" — it recognizes the same two jobs (resource management, abstraction) repeating at other layers. A **hypervisor** (VMware ESXi, KVM) is effectively an OS for operating systems: it resource-manages physical hardware among multiple guest OSes and abstracts it as virtual hardware.

**Containers** (Docker) invert this: they don't virtualize hardware at all — they ask one kernel to abstraction-layer itself into multiple isolated views (namespaces for what a process can see, cgroups for what it can use), so "the OS" a container sees is really an illusion the host kernel maintains.

The interview payoff: when someone asks "is a container a lightweight VM," the precise answer is no — a VM virtualizes hardware under a full guest OS, a container just isolates one shared kernel's namespaces.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in production
slides.markdown:
Cloud platforms are OS concepts scaled up: an AWS EC2 hypervisor resource-manages physical servers among tenants exactly the way an OS resource-manages a CPU among processes, and Kubernetes resource-manages containers across a cluster the way a scheduler resource-manages processes across cores.

When you see "noisy neighbor" problems on shared cloud infrastructure — one tenant's workload degrading another's latency — that's the resource-manager job failing at the hypervisor layer, the same failure mode as a runaway process starving others on a single machine.

Recognizing this pattern lets you reason about unfamiliar systems (a service mesh, a database's connection pool) by asking the same two questions you'd ask of any OS: what's being shared, and what abstraction hides the sharing?
